## The graph knows two facts. Can it suggest a third?

Innopolis University is in Innopolis. Innopolis is in Tatarstan. Both facts are
in our graph, but the direct university-to-region edge is missing. A student
asks whether the university is in Tatarstan. What should our system answer?

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-hero.html >}}

::: {.predict}
**Discuss before continuing.** Does the missing edge mean the claim is false?
What extra ingredient would let us justify the answer?

::: {.predict-answer}
The graph may simply be incomplete. A rule about geographical containment could
justify the third fact. A model trained on similar facts could also suggest it,
but a learned suggestion and a rule-supported conclusion provide different
kinds of evidence.
:::
:::

This lecture develops the prediction approach. We will give entities numerical
representations, use a relation to compare them, and learn which candidate facts
deserve high scores. The difficult part is choosing a comparison that respects
the meaning of the relation. A roommate relationship works in both directions.
An advisor relationship usually does not. One person can advise several students.
The geometry must leave room for these differences.

::: {.w4-thesis}
**The central idea:** a knowledge graph embedding model is a choice about how a
relation compares two entities. That choice determines which patterns are easy
to represent and which create a conflict.
:::

Our four core models are **TransE, TransR, DistMult, and ComplEx**. Each answers
two questions: *where do the embeddings live, and which relation patterns can
their comparison express?* TransE translates in one real space; TransR first
projects into a relation's space; DistMult weights matching real coordinates;
ComplEx uses complex coordinates to distinguish direction.

By the end, you should be able to:

1. Draw the entity and relation spaces of each of these four models.
2. Compute each score by hand and implement it with the correct dimensions.
3. Explain symmetry, direction, inversion, composition, and multiple tails using
   an algebraic construction or a counterexample.
4. Trace a negative sample, loss, and parameter update through a training step.
5. Compute a filtered rank and use a small numerical check to catch a mistake.

The [closing algorithms](#algorithms-you-can-implement) assemble those skills
into complete procedures. RotatE is an optional connection to
[Lab 4](../labs/lab04.qmd), where you rebuild the components in PyTorch.

**Before we begin.** Recall vector addition, multiplication of corresponding
coordinates, and the length of a vector. A matrix makes new coordinates by taking
weighted sums of the old ones. We will introduce complex numbers through pictures.
The diagrams use deliberately simple coordinates, not geographical measurements.

In [Week 3](03-embeddings.qmd), closeness in an embedding space expressed a
notion of node similarity. Today the same pair can fit one relation and fail
another: two people can be colleagues without being roommates. The relation
must therefore participate in the comparison.

The main question stays the same throughout: **what information does a relation preserve, and what
distinctions does its scoring rule erase?**

## 1. A fact becomes a comparison {#from-a-fact-to-three-vectors}

### Three parts, three roles

Read “IU is located in Innopolis” from left to right: an entity, a relation,
and another entity. The relation tells us what the arrow means. Swapping the
endpoints changes the claim to “Innopolis is located in IU.”

::: {#def-w04-kg .definition name="A knowledge graph fact"}
A **triple** $(h,r,t)$ records a head entity $h$, a relation $r$, and a tail
entity $t$. In this lecture, a **knowledge graph** is a set of such triples.
We study relations between two entities; richer graphs can also store dates,
literal values, sources, and qualifiers.
:::

### A knowledge graph preserves the kinds of things and links {#kg-types-and-applications}

Consider a graph of research papers. A paper is written by an author, published
at a venue, and assigned a publication year. An unlabeled drawing would connect
the paper to three neighbors without telling us what any connection means.
That information is essential: an author is a possible answer to “Who wrote
this?”, while a year is a possible answer to “When was it published?”

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-typed.html >}}

There are two kinds of labels to keep separate. A **node type** describes what
an entity is: author, paper, venue, or year. A **relation type** describes an
edge: written_by, published_at, or published_in_year. Multiple node or relation
types make a graph heterogeneous. In the schematic, the year is modeled as a
node; a database could instead store it as a literal attribute. That is a
representation choice, not a change in the underlying fact.

A biomedical graph has a different vocabulary but the same structure. A
hypothetical drug can inhibit a protein; that protein can be associated with a
disease; a candidate treats edge connects a drug to a disease. The path gives
evidence worth investigating, but it does not by itself establish that the drug
treats the disease. The distinction between an observed association and a
justified conclusion matters before any embedding is trained.

These examples explain why knowledge graphs are useful. They combine facts that
would otherwise be separated across tables or documents, and give applications
a vocabulary for asking relational questions. A scholarly search system can
connect an author to their papers and venues. A product system can connect
items to brands, categories, and compatible accessories. A search answer panel
can assemble several facts about one identified entity. Completion is one
operation over this structure; storage, retrieval, provenance, and entity
resolution are other necessary parts of a complete system.

Type constraints can reject obviously unsuitable candidates. A publication year
does not normally answer a query for an author. But type checking cannot choose
the correct person among thousands of authors. The statistical model must learn
distinctions **within** a type as well as between types. If evaluation restricts
candidates by type, that restriction must be stated: it changes the ranking task.

An encoder based on relation-aware message passing could use different learned
transformations for neighbors connected by different
relations. We will study that approach later, in the heterogeneous-GNN material.
For today we use a simpler encoder: directly learn a vector for every entity.
This lets us isolate what the **decoder** contributes, without also changing
how neighborhoods are aggregated.

::: {.predict}
**Read the schema.** A paper has an edge to Ada labeled written_by and an edge
to a venue labeled published_at. What is lost if we erase only the edge labels?
Would keeping the node types recover everything?

::: {.predict-answer}
We lose the meaning of each connection. Types recover some possibilities, but
not all: a person could write, review, or edit a paper, and all three edges have
the same endpoint types. Relation labels carry information beyond node types.
:::
:::

### A large graph is still an incomplete graph {#kg-incompleteness}

The candidate space grows much faster than a list of observed facts. With
$n_e$ entities and $n_r$ relation types there are $n_e^2n_r$ possible ordered
triples before applying schema constraints. Even a toy system with 10,000
entities and 20 relations has two billion possible triples. A stored set of
100,000 facts occupies a very small part of that space.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-incomplete.html >}}

Read the figure one relation at a time. A row fixes the head, a column fixes
the tail, and a cell asks whether that relation connects them. A colored cell
records a known fact. A question mark records our lack of knowledge. A blank
cell is not a measured negative outcome. Adding more relation types gives a
stack of such matrices, often called a three-way adjacency tensor.

Graphs are incomplete for several reasons. Some facts were never collected;
some remain in text; some cannot be linked to a reliable entity identifier;
some need a date or context that the chosen schema omits. More data does not
automatically resolve all these cases. An embedding predicts according to the
facts and conventions it sees, so a systematic collection bias can also become
a systematic prediction bias.

Freebase and its benchmark subsets illustrate this issue.
Other well-known public graph resources include Wikidata, DBpedia, YAGO, and
NELL. The important distinction for our experiments is between a **knowledge
resource** and a **benchmark split extracted from it**. A benchmark does not
make the underlying world complete. Train, validation, and test designate which
recorded facts are available for particular stages of an experiment.

This motivates completion: use regularities in the observed graph to prioritize
unknown cells. A learned model cannot enumerate every possible fact during
training. It samples comparisons, shares parameters across facts, and later
scores a selected query's candidates. We will examine each step separately.

### Learn representations, then choose the comparison

An embedding assigns a short list of learned numbers to each entity. IU has one
vector; Innopolis has another. The same entity vector is reused wherever that
entity appears. Relations also have learned parameters. They tell the model
how to compare the two entity vectors for a particular kind of fact.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-lookup.html >}}

There are two decisions here. The **encoder** retrieves the representations.
The **decoder**, also called the scorer, uses them to judge a triple. We use
simple embedding lookup, so no graph neural network is needed. Most of today's
models share that encoder and differ in the decoder.

The vectors do not begin with a meaning such as “latitude” or “university size.”
Training adjusts them so that many observed facts become compatible at once.
Two coordinates are enough to draw our examples; real models use more. An entity's
integer ID only identifies its row in the embedding table. Changing the ID
consistently does not change the entity or its relationships.

If there are $n_e$ entities and each has $d$ real coordinates, the entity table
contains $n_ed$ learned numbers. Looking up a triple retrieves two entity rows
and the relevant relation parameters. The scorer returns one number. A new
scorer can therefore be compared with an old one while holding the graph,
queries, and lookup procedure fixed.

This is a **shallow, transductive** representation: a training-time ID owns a
learned row. A previously unseen entity has no trained row merely because its
name has appeared at inference time. Incorporating it requires additional data,
optimization, or an encoder that can construct a representation from attributes
or neighborhoods. This is one reason not to confuse embedding lookup with a
general-purpose language or graph encoder.

The coordinate axes are also not uniquely interpretable. For TransE, adding
the same vector to every entity leaves every residual unchanged because that
shift cancels between head and tail. An orthogonal change of coordinates applied
to all entity and relation vectors preserves Euclidean distances. The model's
predictions can be stable even though the displayed coordinates look different.
What matters is the relation among vectors, not the name of an axis.

### Completion means ranking possible answers

Suppose we hide the tail of a fact. For $(\text{IU},\text{located\_in},?)$,
the model tries candidate tails and scores each completed triple. It then returns
the highest-scoring candidates for inspection.

::: {#def-w04-scoring .definition name="Completion as ranking"}
A **scoring function** $f(h,r,t)$ assigns one real number to a triple.
Throughout this lecture, **higher is better**. Tail prediction ranks candidates
for $(h,r,?)$; head prediction ranks candidates for $(?,r,t)$.
:::

This shared convention will keep the models comparable in our reasoning. A
distance-based model will negate its distance, making a small error a high score.
A compatibility model will reward agreement directly. Their numerical scales
can differ; their job is to order candidate answers well.

An unrecorded triple is **unknown** under the open-world assumption. It may be
false, or it may be a true fact that nobody entered. We will still need sampled
comparisons for training, but sampling a replacement does not establish that it
is false. Likewise, a high score expresses learned plausibility, not a proof or
an automatically calibrated probability.

Keep three related tasks distinct. **Tail prediction** holds the head and
relation fixed and varies the tail. **Head prediction** holds the relation and
tail fixed and varies the head. **Relation prediction** holds both entities
fixed and asks which relation best describes them. Ordinary untyped link
prediction asks whether an edge connects a pair at all. KG completion also
needs the edge's meaning. Our lab evaluates both head and tail prediction.

**The next question:** what is the simplest geometric action a relation could take?

## 2. TransE makes a relation a shared displacement

### Move the head, then inspect the miss

Put IU at $\mathbf h=(1,1)$. Let the relation vector be $\mathbf r=(2,1)$.
Read that relation as an instruction: move two units right and one unit up.
Starting from IU, it predicts a tail at $(3,2)$.

We place Innopolis at $(3,2)$ and a comparison candidate, Kazan, at $(3,1)$.
The first point is an exact landing; the second misses by one unit. Before
looking at the score, the picture already tells us which candidate should win.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-transe.html >}}

Use the control to choose Kazan. The head and relation stay fixed; only the
candidate being judged changes. Now lower the relation's vertical component to
zero. The prediction lands on Kazan instead. This is how a relation vector
affects a ranking: it changes the place against which every tail is compared.

The calculation has three meaningful steps. Add head and relation to locate the
prediction. Subtract the candidate tail to obtain the **residual**, or miss.
Measure that residual's length. Negate the distance to obey our higher-is-better
score convention.

$$
f(h,r,t)=-\|\mathbf h+\mathbf r-\mathbf t\|_2.
$$ {#eq-w04-transe}

Here $\mathbf h$, $\mathbf r$, and $\mathbf t$ are real vectors of the same
dimension. The Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ measures length. Innopolis receives
score $0$; Kazan receives $-1$. The closer tail wins because $0>-1$.
This model is **TransE**: a relation acts as a translation.

::: {.predict}
**Calculate one new case.** Keep $\mathbf h=(1,1)$ and $\mathbf r=(2,1)$.
A candidate tail is at $(0,6)$. What is the miss, its length, and the score?

::: {.predict-answer}
The prediction remains $(3,2)$. Subtracting the tail gives $(3,-4)$, whose
length is $5$. The score is $-5$. A large positive distance becomes a low score.
:::
:::

### One relation must work for many facts

The relation vector belongs to the relation type, not to an individual edge.
Every fact with that relation uses the same displacement. That sharing is what
makes generalization possible: observations about one entity affect how other
entities are compared. It also creates constraints.

If one relation needed a different arrow for every fact, fitting a stored graph
would be easy but would tell us little about a missing fact. TransE makes a much
stronger bet: one shared arrow can organize many facts. Training will try to
find entity positions and arrows that make that bet work.

The original model supports different distance choices. We use Euclidean distance
throughout these examples and the lab. Zero distance means an exact geometric
fit. It does not certify that the fact is true, and learning a useful ranking
does not require every positive fact to reach zero distance.

### What would a successful learned geometry look like? {#transe-parallel-displacements}

Imagine three observed pairs with the same relation. A successful TransE
geometry gives them approximately parallel displacements of approximately equal
length. It does not require their head vectors to coincide. The relation is
reused; each head supplies a different starting point.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-parallel.html >}}

For the first pair, subtract the head from the tail: $(2,1)-(0,0)=(2,1)$.
For the second, $(2,3)-(0,2)=(2,1)$. For the third,
$(5,1)-(3,0)=(2,1)$. All three constraints agree on one relation vector.
This is the pattern the optimizer is trying to create across many observations.

If the observed displacements disagree, the model must move entities, move the
relation, or accept residual error. Moving one entity can help one fact while
hurting another because the row is shared. A two-dimensional picture of a
trained embedding is therefore evidence about a coupled optimization problem,
not a collection of independent arrows. A visualization of higher-dimensional
embeddings also introduces a second projection whose distortions must not be
mistaken for the model's original distances.

In our two-dimensional examples, the $L_1$ norm would measure the sum of the
absolute horizontal and vertical misses; $L_2$ measures straight-line length.
For residual $(3,4)$ they give 7 and 5 respectively. Both reward smaller error,
but their equal-distance contours differ. Keep the choice fixed when checking
hand calculations against an implementation. The scorer, loss, and normalization
are separate choices in the full learning procedure.

**Before choosing a more complicated model, we should find a fact pattern that
the shared-arrow idea struggles to represent.**

## 3. The graph puts demands on the geometry

### The same arrow does not always mean the same kind of relationship

A relation name carries expectations about other facts. If Ada is Bo's roommate,
the reverse roommate fact should also hold. If Ada advises Bo, the reverse
advisor fact need not hold. An inverse relation would use a different name:
Bo is advised by Ada. These distinctions become tests of our scorer.

::: {#def-w04-pattern .definition name="A relation pattern"}
A **relation pattern** describes how facts constrain other facts. We will test
symmetry, direction, inverse relations, composition, and multiple valid tails.
The graph states the desired pattern; a model supplies a geometry that may or
may not accommodate it.
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-atlas.html >}}

Read the atlas as five separate questions. Must an edge reverse under the same
relation? Must its reverse be rejected? Does a different relation undo it?
Does a declared rule connect the ends of a path? Can a single query have several
correct answers? Passing one test does not imply passing the others.

The direction row uses **asymmetry**: both directions cannot hold together.
Strictly, *antisymmetry* allows both only for an entity related to itself.
KG papers sometimes use “antisymmetry” more loosely for distinguishing forward
and reverse. Our arguments will state the actual score or distance condition.

Here is a precise way to read the five questions. Symmetry asks whether
$r(a,b)\Rightarrow r(b,a)$. An inverse relation asks whether
$r_1(a,b)\Rightarrow r_2(b,a)$ with a possibly different relation name.
Composition asks whether $r_1(a,b)\land r_2(b,c)\Rightarrow r_3(a,c)$.
Transitivity is the special case where all three relation names are the same.
A one-to-many example supplies two facts $r(h,t_1)$ and $r(h,t_2)$ with distinct
tail entities. These are statements about facts; we still have to say what
counts as representing them with scores.

We will use three levels of argument. An **exact fit** asks a distance to be
zero. A **score identity** holds for every parameter choice, whether trained
or not. A **ranking experiment** checks whether true candidates beat alternatives
after learning. Exact constructions explain geometric possibilities, and score
identities expose unavoidable restrictions. Neither substitutes for the ranking
experiment. Keeping these levels separate is how to read a capability table
without turning a useful schematic into an unjustified universal claim.

### A symmetric pair reveals TransE's conflict

On a line, put Ada at 0 and Bo at 2. A translation of $+2$ reaches Bo from Ada.
Apply that same translation to Bo: it lands at 4, farther from Ada. To return
to Ada we would need $-2$, but the roommate relation must keep the same vector.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-collapse.html >}}

::: {.predict}
**Try to repair the drawing.** Can you place the two people at different points
and choose one translation that takes each exactly to the other?

::: {.predict-answer}
No. The two journeys need opposite displacements. Requiring the same displacement
in both directions forces it to zero and places the two embeddings together.
:::
:::

::: {#prp-transe-sym .proposition name="Exact symmetric TransE fits collapse"}
If both directions have zero distance, then
$\mathbf a+\mathbf r=\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf b+\mathbf r=\mathbf a$.
Adding the equations gives $2\mathbf r=0$, so $\mathbf r=0$ and
$\mathbf a=\mathbf b$.
:::

The important phrase is **both distances are zero**. This is a statement about
exact fitting with distinct embeddings. A trained TransE model may compromise,
keep small nonzero errors, and still rank useful answers highly. We have diagnosed
a geometric pressure; we have not predicted the outcome of every training run.

Multiple tails expose a related pressure. If an advisor has two students, an
exact TransE fit asks both student vectors to equal the same predicted point:
$\mathbf t_1=\mathbf h+\mathbf r=\mathbf t_2$. Distinct IDs survive, but their
vectors coincide. The reverse case, several heads sharing one tail, creates a
similar constraint on the heads.

### Direction works because the reverse adds the shift again {#transe-direction-inversion}

Suppose a forward edge fits exactly, so $\mathbf t=\mathbf h+\mathbf r$.
The reverse residual is then

$$
\mathbf t+\mathbf r-\mathbf h
=(\mathbf h+\mathbf r)+\mathbf r-\mathbf h=2\mathbf r.
$$

For any nonzero relation vector, the forward distance is zero and the reverse
distance is $2\|\mathbf r\|_2$. With $\mathbf r=(2,1)$ the reverse score is
$-2\sqrt5$. This is a construction of directional behavior. The model does
not need a separate mechanism to notice that “parent of” should differ from
its reversal; a nonzero translation already permits that distinction.

### An inverse relation undoes the shift

For an inverse relation, we are allowed a different vector. If the first
relation moves two units right and one unit up, its inverse moves two left and
one down. Thus $\mathbf r_{\rm inv}=-\mathbf r$ gives

$$
\mathbf t+\mathbf r_{\rm inv}
=(\mathbf h+\mathbf r)-\mathbf r=\mathbf h.
$$

Using the same vector is symmetry; negating it is inversion. The distinction
matters in the data: advisor and advised_by name different relations, whereas
roommate uses the same name on the reverse edge. Ordinary training does not
automatically tie inverse vectors together, even when this construction exists.
One can impose such a constraint when the inverse relation is known, or examine
whether the learned vectors approximately satisfy it.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-path.html >}}

### Composition adds displacements, with a visible error budget {#transe-composition}

In the second part of the figure, take $\mathbf a=(0,0)$,
$\mathbf b=(2,1)$, and $\mathbf c=(3,3)$. The first step uses
$\mathbf r_1=(2,1)$ and the second uses $\mathbf r_2=(1,2)$.
The direct displacement is $(3,3)=\mathbf r_1+\mathbf r_2$. Substituting the
first exact fit into the second eliminates the intermediate entity:

$$
\mathbf c=\mathbf b+\mathbf r_2
=(\mathbf a+\mathbf r_1)+\mathbf r_2
=\mathbf a+(\mathbf r_1+\mathbf r_2).
$$

Setting $\mathbf r_3=\mathbf r_1+\mathbf r_2$ makes the direct edge exact.
That relation identity is sufficient for this geometric construction. It is
not a statement that arbitrary learned relation rows are automatically linked.

The approximate case explains what the drawing does and does not promise.
Write the two residuals as $\mathbf e_1=\mathbf a+\mathbf r_1-\mathbf b$
and $\mathbf e_2=\mathbf b+\mathbf r_2-\mathbf c$. If the direct relation
is their vector sum, its residual is $\mathbf e_1+\mathbf e_2$. By the triangle
inequality its length is at most $\|\mathbf e_1\|+\|\mathbf e_2\|$.
Errors can accumulate along a path. If $\mathbf r_3$ also differs from the
sum, that relation mismatch adds another error term. A promising path does not
become a logical proof merely because its edge scores are high.

For the opening containment example, two steps of located_in add
$2\mathbf r$, not $\mathbf r$. Requiring all three edges of that same-relation
triangle to fit exactly forces $2\mathbf r=\mathbf r$, hence $\mathbf r=0$.
Composing two relations and making one relation transitive are distinct demands.

### Several close tails are weaker than several distinct exact fits

If both tails are within distance $\epsilon$ of the same predicted point,
their separation is at most $2\epsilon$. To see it, travel from the first tail
to the prediction and from the prediction to the second tail; the direct route
cannot be longer. Therefore, insisting on tiny positive distances pressures
several true tails toward one another. Allowing nonzero distances permits
distinct tails and useful rankings, but it does not remove this pressure.

This also explains why equidistant tails can remain distinct: two points
can lie on the same circle around a prediction and receive equal scores. They
need not coincide unless both distances must be zero. Later we will compare
these circular score contours with DistMult's straight ones.

::: {.predict}
**Classify the requirement.** An advisor has two students, each student is
advised_by that advisor, and the students are roommates. Which part asks for
one-to-many behavior, which asks for an inverse, and which asks for symmetry?

::: {.predict-answer}
One advisor with two student tails is one-to-many. Reversing advisor into
advised_by uses an inverse relation. Reversing roommate keeps the same relation
and asks for symmetry. The graph can demand all three at once, so checking
only one property of a model is insufficient.
:::
:::

**A useful repair:** let a relation compare only the features it needs, while
keeping the full entity representations distinct.

## 4. TransR changes the space in which a relation acts {#transr-give-each-relation-its-own-view}

### Distinct entities can look the same to one relation

Two students may share an advisor but have different research interests. A
relation about their advisor need not use every feature that a relation about
their research uses. TransR gives each relation a learned linear map, applies it
to both entity vectors, and then translates in the resulting space.

Watch the two tails below. They begin at $(2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$. The left-hand
picture stores the entities. The right-hand picture shows what this particular
relation sees. Lower the vertical scale and notice which picture changes.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-transr.html >}}

At scale one, both tails miss the predicted point $(2,0)$ by one unit. At scale
zero, the map discards their vertical difference. Both projected tails now land
at $(2,0)$, while the original entity vectors remain distinct. A different
relation can use a different map and retain the distinction.

This is a selective loss of information. A decoy at $(-1,0)$ still projects to
$(-1,0)$ and remains three units away. A map that collapsed everything would also
erase that useful distinction. The model needs to learn which differences are
relevant to each relation, not merely make all distances small.

### Project both endpoints, then translate

Let $M_r$ be the matrix for relation $r$. First form $M_r\mathbf h$ and
$M_r\mathbf t$. These are the head and tail as seen by that relation. Then use
the same translation idea as before:

$$
f(h,r,t)=-\|M_r\mathbf h+\mathbf r-M_r\mathbf t\|_2.
$$ {#eq-w04-transr}

Entities have $d$ coordinates, projected entities have $k$, and
$M_r\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}$. The translation $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^k$
lives in the projected space. Both endpoints use the same matrix. A general
linear map can mix or scale coordinates; “projection” here need not mean an
orthogonal projection.

The widget uses $M_r=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$. It keeps the first
coordinate and scales the second by $\lambda$. At zero, differences along the
vertical direction become invisible to this relation. Such invisible directions
form the matrix's **kernel**. The term names something you have already seen
in the picture.

::: {.predict}
**Transfer the idea.** A different relation keeps only the vertical coordinate:
$M_r=[0\;1]$. Its head is $(5,1)$ and its translation is $2$. Which tails fit
exactly: $(0,3)$, $(7,3)$, or $(5,4)$?

::: {.predict-answer}
The projected head is 1, so the predicted projected tail is 3. The first two
tails project to 3 and have score 0. The third projects to 4 and has score −1.
Horizontal differences do not matter to this relation.
:::
:::

### The kernel describes exactly which differences disappear {#transr-kernel}

Take $M=[1\;0]$. Every vector $(0,v)$ maps to zero. These vertical vectors
form $\ker M$, the set of inputs that the map erases. They are **differences**
that the relation cannot detect. The set of points that map to 2 is instead
$\{(2,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$: a vertical line shifted away from the origin.
Do not confuse that shifted set with the kernel itself.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-kernel.html >}}

Both $(2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$ map to 2 because their difference $(0,2)$ lies in
the kernel. A second relation using $[0\;1]$ would map them to 1 and −1 and
could distinguish them. There is one entity table, but each relation decides
which of its distinctions matter. The matrix learns a view of the entities;
it does not create a new entity ID for every occurrence.

In general, if $M_r\mathbf t_0=M_r\mathbf h+\mathbf r$, then
$\mathbf t_0+\mathbf v$ is another exact tail whenever $M_r\mathbf v=0$:

$$
M_r(\mathbf t_0+\mathbf v)
=M_r\mathbf t_0+M_r\mathbf v
=M_r\mathbf h+\mathbf r.
$$

The whole set of exact tails is a translated kernel, often called an affine
fiber. A nontrivial kernel gives the relation room to accept different stored
entities at the same projected location. If the map is injective, its kernel
contains only zero and this particular source of flexibility disappears.
For a $k\times d$ matrix, rank-nullity says
$\dim\ker M_r=d-\operatorname{rank}(M_r)$: directions retained and directions
erased account for the entire entity space.

### Symmetry, direction, and inversion have different constructions {#transr-pattern-constructions}

For **symmetry**, use the two distinct entities $(2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$,
projection $[1\;0]$, and translation 0. Both projected entities equal 2,
so both directed distances are zero. The original vectors remain distinct.
The same construction also gives zero distance to self-pairs: it establishes
the symmetric-pair fit, not a perfect representation of every desired negative
in an arbitrary graph.

For **direction**, keep $[1\;0]$ but use head $(0,0)$, tail $(2,1)$, and
translation 2. The forward projected residual is $0+2-2=0$; the reverse is
$2+2-0=4$. The algebra is the TransE argument inside the relation space:
an exact forward fit and a nonzero translation produce reverse residual
$2\mathbf r$.

For **inversion**, use the same projection in both relations and negate the
translation. In the previous example the reverse relation uses −2, giving
$2-2-0=0$. In symbols, $M_2=M_1$ and $\mathbf r_2=-\mathbf r_1$ are
sufficient to undo the projected shift. If the two matrices are unrelated,
negating the relation vector alone is not enough: the starting and ending
coordinates may mean different things in the two spaces.

For **one-to-many**, return to the slider example: both tails have the same
projection, which matches the translated head. Many-to-one follows the same
logic with multiple projected heads. These constructions represent several
relation patterns without requiring the original entity vectors to
collapse. They do require the learned map to preserve enough information to
reject unsuitable alternatives.

### Compose constraints by tracking the information each step loses {#transr-composition-proof}

The statement “linear maps compose” does not by itself explain TransR
composition. Each relation maps **both**
endpoints from entity space into its own comparison space. Multiplying two
arbitrary projection matrices can even be dimensionally undefined. We need
to combine the constraints they impose on endpoint differences.

Start with a concrete three-coordinate example. Let
$\mathbf a=(0,1,7)$, $\mathbf b=(2,1,4)$, and $\mathbf c=(5,8,4)$.
The first relation keeps the first two coordinates and translates by $(2,0)$.
The second keeps the first and third coordinates and translates by $(3,0)$.
The direct relation can keep the first coordinate, set its second output to
zero, and translate by $(5,0)$.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-kernel-compose.html >}}

Verify each step. Under $M_1$, the endpoints become $(0,1)$ and $(2,1)$.
Under $M_2$, they become $(2,4)$ and $(5,4)$. The first step ignores the change
in the third entity coordinate; the second ignores the change in the second.
Only the first coordinate carries a shared constraint from start to finish:
it must increase by $2+3=5$. Under $M_3$, the original endpoints become
$(0,0)$ and $(5,0)$, so the direct fit is exact.

Now derive that result without relying on these particular coordinates.
Assume two exact fits and choose entity-space offsets $\mathbf g_1,\mathbf g_2$
such that $M_1\mathbf g_1=\mathbf r_1$ and
$M_2\mathbf g_2=\mathbf r_2$. Such offsets exist when the relation vectors
are in the images of their maps, as they must be for the assumed exact fits.

**Step 1: describe every allowed first step.** Rearrange the first fit:

$$
M_1(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\mathbf r_1=M_1\mathbf g_1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf b=\mathbf a+\mathbf g_1+\mathbf v_1,
\qquad \mathbf v_1\in\ker M_1.
$$

The vector $\mathbf g_1$ supplies the required displacement. The kernel vector
$\mathbf v_1$ supplies any additional displacement that relation 1 cannot see.
The same reasoning gives
$\mathbf c=\mathbf b+\mathbf g_2+\mathbf v_2$ with
$\mathbf v_2\in\ker M_2$.

**Step 2: eliminate the intermediate entity.** Substitute the first expression
for $\mathbf b$ into the second:

$$
\mathbf c-\mathbf a
=\mathbf g_1+\mathbf g_2+\mathbf v_1+\mathbf v_2.
$$

All uncertainty in the endpoint difference lies in
$S=\ker M_1+\ker M_2$, the set of sums of one vector from each kernel.
The plus sign between subspaces means this set of sums; it is not merely their
union and not the intersection of their invisible directions.

**Step 3: make the direct relation ignore that uncertainty.** Choose a matrix
$M_3$ whose kernel is $S$, and set
$\mathbf r_3=M_3(\mathbf g_1+\mathbf g_2)$. Applying it to the endpoint
difference erases $\mathbf v_1+\mathbf v_2$, leaving

$$
M_3(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=\mathbf r_3
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M_3\mathbf a+\mathbf r_3=M_3\mathbf c.
$$ {#eq-w04-transr-composition}

Why can $M_3$ have the same $k\times d$ shape? The subspace $S$ contains
$\ker M_1$, so its codimension is at most $\operatorname{rank}(M_1)\leq k$.
Choose rows spanning the orthogonal complement of $S$, then pad with zero rows
until there are $k$ rows. The resulting kernel is exactly $S$. This completes
the construction rather than assuming that an appropriate map appears by magic.

The cost of this construction is visible in the example: the composed relation
discards more information. If the two kernels together span all of entity
space, $M_3$ becomes zero and the composed relation distinguishes nothing.
Representing a path implication is useful only if enough distinctions survive
to reject relevant negatives. Learning is also not guaranteed to discover these
particular tied maps and offsets unless the training objective encourages them.

::: {.predict}
**Find the surviving information.** In the three-coordinate example, could the
composed relation reject $(5,-100,100)$ as a tail for the same head?

::: {.predict-answer}
Not with $M_3$ keeping only the first coordinate. That tail also maps to $(5,0)$
and fits exactly. The endpoint constraint inherited from the two steps concerns
only the first coordinate. Additional evidence or constraints would be needed
to distinguish these candidates.
:::
:::

The flexibility costs something. Every relation now stores a matrix as well as
a vector, and each score requires two projections. A sparse relation has more
parameters to estimate from limited evidence. That motivates a different approach:
compare feature agreement with a small number of relation weights.

## 5. DistMult rewards agreement, but loses direction {#distmult-and-complex-compare-compatible-features}

### A score can measure compatibility directly

So far, we have asked a relation to predict a location. DistMult asks a different
question: how well do the head and tail's features agree, after weighting those
features for the relation?

Take $\mathbf h=(2,1)$, $\mathbf r=(1,3)$, and $\mathbf t=(1,2)$.
The first coordinate contributes $2\times1\times1=2$. The second contributes
$1\times3\times2=6$. Adding the contributions gives a score of 8. A positive
relation weight rewards same-sign agreement; a negative weight reverses it.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-bilinear.html >}}

Start with **DistMult** selected. Change the second relation weight. You can make
its contribution larger, remove it, or reverse its sign. Each change still
produces one score by adding coordinate contributions.

$$
f(h,r,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_i r_i t_i.
$$ {#eq-w04-distmult}

The subscript $i$ selects a coordinate. The sum combines all $d$ contributions.
An alternative view is a dot product between the transformed head
$\mathbf h\circ\mathbf r$ and the tail, where $\circ$ means multiplication
of corresponding coordinates. No distance is being measured, and the score
does not have TransE's upper bound of zero.

### Why start with a matrix, then remove its off-diagonal entries? {#distmult-bilinear-matrix}

A general bilinear score is $\mathbf h^T A_r\mathbf t$, with a relation matrix
$A_r$. Expanding it gives $\sum_i\sum_j h_i A_{r,ij}t_j$: every head feature
can interact with every tail feature. “Bilinear” means linear in the head when
the relation and tail are fixed, and linear in the tail when the other two are
fixed. It does not mean linear in all unknown parameters simultaneously.

Use our head $(2,1)$ and tail $(1,2)$ with
$A_r=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$.
First multiply $A_r\mathbf t=(5,6)$, then take the head's dot product:
$2\times5+1\times6=16$. In reverse, $A_r\mathbf h=(4,3)$ and
$\mathbf t^T A_r\mathbf h=1\times4+2\times3=10$.
The off-diagonal entry lets a first head coordinate interact differently with
a second tail coordinate than in the reversed pair.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-bilinear-matrix.html >}}

DistMult restricts $A_r$ to the diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf r)$.
Deleting that off-diagonal 2 removes a contribution of
$h_1\times2\times t_2=8$ from the forward score. The score becomes 8, matching
our original calculation. All cross-coordinate terms disappear; each remaining
term compares the same coordinate in the head and tail.

This is a statistical and computational tradeoff. A full matrix has $d^2$
relation parameters and generally costs $O(d^2)$ to apply. A diagonal matrix
has $d$ parameters and costs $O(d)$. With limited evidence for a relation, the
larger matrix can fit accidental correlations. Restricting it makes estimation
and scoring cheaper, but also removes distinctions we may need. We should test
which distinctions are lost before deciding that the smaller model is sufficient.

### The decisive test is to swap the endpoints

::: {.predict}
**Predict before using the checkbox.** Swap the head and tail while keeping the
relation fixed. Will 8 increase, decrease, or stay the same? Could more training
change that answer?

::: {.predict-answer}
It stays 8. Each coordinate multiplies the same three real numbers in a different
order. Training can change the numbers but cannot change that identity.
:::
:::

::: {#prp-distmult-sym .proposition name="DistMult forces equal reverse scores"}
For every choice of parameters,
$f(h,r,t)=\sum_i h_i r_i t_i=\sum_i t_i r_i h_i=f(t,r,h)$.
:::

This is useful for a symmetric relation such as roommate. It is a problem when
the graph needs to distinguish “Kazan is the capital of Tatarstan” from its
reverse. Both triples receive the same score under the same relation, regardless
of how long we train.

### Alignment is related to cosine similarity, but also depends on length {#distmult-level-sets}

Let $\mathbf q=\mathbf h\circ\mathbf r$. Then the score is
$\mathbf q^T\mathbf t$. For nonzero vectors, this can be written as

$$
f(h,r,t)=\|\mathbf q\|_2\,\|\mathbf t\|_2\cos\angle(\mathbf q,\mathbf t).
$$

The angle describes alignment; the lengths multiply that alignment. The raw
score is therefore not normalized cosine similarity. For $\mathbf q=(2,0)$,
tails $(1,0)$ and $(10,0)$ have the same angle and cosine of 1, but scores 2
and 20. Increasing a vector's length can increase the score without changing
its direction. This is one reason to choose regularization deliberately.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-levelsets.html >}}

Now consider two tails $(2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$. Both have score 4 against
$\mathbf q=(2,0)$. In fact, every tail $(2,v)$ has score 4. A fixed-score
condition $\mathbf q^T\mathbf t=c$ describes a line in two dimensions, or
a hyperplane in higher dimensions when $\mathbf q\ne0$. It can contain many
distinct entity vectors. A threshold $\mathbf q^T\mathbf t>c$ selects a
half-space. In this geometry, accepting several tails does not require their
coordinates to coincide.

Compare that with TransE in the left panel. Distinct tails can share a nonzero
distance on a circle, but shrinking that distance to zero leaves a single point.
The difference between the two geometries is a difference in their score
contours. It is more informative than saying that one model “supports many
tails” without stating the score condition.

### Inverse names cannot repair a direction-blind scorer {#distmult-inverse-composition}

Suppose Ada advises Bo. We want advisor(Ada, Bo) and advised_by(Bo, Ada) to
score highly, while their respective reversals score poorly. Setting both
relation vectors equal can make the two desired scores agree. But DistMult
also equates each score with its own unwanted reversal. Two relation names do
not undo the scorer's inability to tell head from tail.

The obstacle is the required directional distinction, not merely that inverse
relations should have different-looking parameter vectors. Different vectors
can produce the same scores on a restricted collection of entity embeddings.
When diagnosing a representation, specify the facts and negatives that must
be separated; an argument about parameter names alone is insufficient.

Composition needs similar care. Diagonal matrices can be multiplied, and the
original DistMult work uses relation embeddings in rule mining. That is different
from proving that two high pairwise scores force a high score at the path's ends.
Here is a counterexample to that universal implication:

$$
\mathbf a=(1,0),\quad \mathbf b=(1,1),\quad \mathbf c=(0,1),
\qquad \mathbf r_1=\mathbf r_2=\mathbf r_3=(1,1).
$$

Both path scores are 1, while the direct score is 0. Even choosing the direct
diagonal matrix as the product of the two identity matrices has not changed
this. For a threshold of 0.5, both premises pass and the conclusion fails.
The reason is that a high dot product does not say
$\mathbf a\circ\mathbf r_1=\mathbf b$; there is no such point equality to
substitute into the next step. Directed compositions additionally encounter
DistMult's reversal restriction.

This explains the limits of the scoring rule without claiming
that DistMult can never learn a dataset containing compositional regularities.
Its strength is a small, efficient compatibility function. Its fixed weakness
is reversal symmetry. The next model keeps coordinate-wise products while
making the two endpoint roles distinguishable.

## 6. ComplEx makes the two directions distinguishable

### A complex coordinate is a pair of real numbers

Write $a+bi$ as a point with coordinates $(a,b)$, where $i^2=-1$. The horizontal
coordinate is its real part and the vertical coordinate is its imaginary part.
We will use two operations. **Conjugation** reflects the point across the real
axis: $\overline{a+bi}=a-bi$. Multiplication by $i$ makes a quarter-turn:
$(a+bi)i=-b+ai$.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-conjugate.html >}}

Ordinary multiplication distributes over both parts:
$(a+bi)(c+di)=ac+adi+bci+bd,i^2$.
Because $i^2=-1$, collect the real and imaginary terms to obtain
$(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i$. For example,
$(1+2i)(3+i)=3+i+6i-2=1+7i$.
Nothing here requires an unfamiliar numerical data type conceptually: we can
store two real arrays and implement these additions and products ourselves.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-rotation.html >}}

Follow the specific point $(1,1)$. A quarter-turn takes it to $(-1,1)$, so
$(1+i)i=-1+i$. Applying the same turn again takes it to $(-1,-1)$, not back
to the starting point. Complex multiplication gives us a simple way to construct
a transformation with different forward and reverse behavior.

### The score compares the transformed head with the tail

Use $h=1+i$, $r=i$, and $t=-1+i$. Forward, the transformed head $hr$ points
exactly along the tail. Reverse, the transformed head $tr$ points opposite the
original head. The following diagram makes the comparison visible.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-complex.html >}}

The **ComplEx** score multiplies by the conjugate tail and takes the real part.
For this example, $hr=-1+i$ and $\bar t=-1-i$. Their product is 2, so the
forward score is 2. In reverse, $tr=-1-i$ and $\bar h=1-i$. Their product is
−2, so the reverse score is −2.

$$
f(h,r,t)=\operatorname{Re}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_i r_i\bar t_i\right).
$$ {#eq-w04-complex}

The coordinates are now complex. The bar conjugates the tail, the sum combines
coordinate contributions, and $\operatorname{Re}$ keeps the real part so the
result can rank candidates. One complex coordinate stores two real numbers.

Why does the picture use alignment? For two complex numbers $z=a+bi$ and
$w=u+vi$, the real part of $z\bar w$ is $au+bv$. That is the ordinary dot
product of the two coordinate pairs. The conjugate turns complex multiplication
into this familiar real comparison. ComplEx combines such comparisons after
transforming the head by the relation.

Return to the [coordinate-products experiment](#w4-bi-widget) and select **ComplEx**. Its two
boxes now show real-channel and imaginary-channel contributions. Swap the
endpoints and watch the score change sign. Then set the imaginary relation
component to zero. In this particular example the whole relation becomes zero,
and both scores become zero.

::: {.predict}
**Explain the mechanism.** Why would removing the conjugate from the score
restore the same score in both directions?

::: {.predict-answer}
Without conjugation, $hrt$ and $trh$ contain the same complex factors. Complex
scalar multiplication commutes, so their real parts agree. The asymmetric use
of conjugation is essential to this construction.
:::
:::

::: {#prp-complex .proposition name="ComplEx can also represent symmetry"}
A real relation vector makes the score symmetric, even with complex entity
vectors. Imaginary relation components permit asymmetric terms. They do not
force every entity pair to have different forward and reverse scores.
:::

The lesson is not that every relation should become asymmetric. A useful model
must allow the graph to determine which relations need symmetry and which need
direction. ComplEx offers both possibilities. The cost is a second real channel
per complex coordinate, which matters when comparing model sizes.

### Expand the score until the direction becomes visible {#complex-four-term-derivation}

The quarter-turn example proves that a directional pair is possible. To see
which parameters control it in general, work on one complex coordinate. Write
$h=a+bi$, $r=c+di$, and $t=u+vi$. First transform the head:

$$
hr=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i.
$$

Now multiply by $\bar t=u-vi$. The real part contains the product of the two
real components and the contribution from $i\times(-i)=1$:

$$
\operatorname{Re}(hr\bar t)
=(ac-bd)u+(ad+bc)v
=acu+adv+bcv-bdu.
$$ {#eq-w04-complex-four-terms}

Read the four terms as four real feature interactions. The first uses real
head, real relation, and real tail. The second uses real head, imaginary
relation, and imaginary tail. The third uses imaginary head, real relation,
and imaginary tail. The fourth uses imaginary head, imaginary relation, and
real tail, with a minus sign. The full score sums these contributions over
all complex coordinates. Taking the real part is essential: the ranking must
compare real numbers.

Group the same expression by the relation's two components:

$$
\underbrace{c(au+bv)}_{S:\ \text{shared on reversal}}
\; + \;
\underbrace{d(av-bu)}_{A:\ \text{changes sign on reversal}}.
$$ {#eq-w04-complex-symmetric-skew}

Swapping $(a,b)$ with $(u,v)$ leaves $au+bv$ unchanged and negates $av-bu$.
Thus the forward score is $S+A$ and the reverse score is $S-A$. Their difference
is $2A$. This decomposition makes the mechanism explicit: the real part of the
relation weights a symmetric contribution, while its imaginary part weights
a contribution that changes sign when the endpoints swap.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-complex-parts.html >}}

The experiment uses $h=1+2i$ and $t=3+i$, so $au+bv=5$ and $av-bu=-5$.
The two scores are $5c-5d$ and $5c+5d$. Begin with $d=0$: changing $c$ moves
both scores together. Then change $d$: the scores separate in opposite
directions. Try $c=1,d=-1$ and obtain forward 10, reverse 0. Conjugating the
relation reverses the sign of $d$ and exchanges those scores.

### Symmetry and asymmetry follow from the decomposition {#complex-symmetry-proof}

If every imaginary relation component is zero, every $A$ term vanishes and
the score is symmetric. This proves the earlier proposition for arbitrary
complex entity vectors. The entities do not need to be real; only the relation
is restricted. If the entities and relations are all real, the score reduces
to DistMult exactly.

If every real relation component is zero, every $S$ term vanishes and the
forward and reverse scores are negatives of one another. Positive values in
one direction can be paired with negative values in the other. A mixed relation
can combine both effects. This is more flexible than imposing symmetry on every
relation in the graph.

An imaginary relation does not guarantee a nonzero directional difference for
every pair. If the two real coordinate pairs are parallel, $av-bu=0$ and that
coordinate contributes no asymmetry. Contributions can also cancel across
coordinates. The model permits the required behavior; learned entity geometry
still determines which pairs exhibit it.

### An inverse relation conjugates the relation parameters {#complex-inverse-proof}

To reverse an entire relation's score function, set
$\mathbf r_{\rm inv}=\overline{\mathbf r}$. This keeps its symmetric part
and flips its directional part. Swapping endpoints also flips the directional
part, so the two sign changes cancel:

$$
f(h,r,t)=f(t,\bar r,h).
$$

The identity can also be checked directly. The complex conjugate of
$t\bar r\bar h$ is $\bar t r h$, which equals $hr\bar t$ because scalar
complex multiplication commutes. A number and its conjugate have the same real
part. Apply that argument coordinate by coordinate and sum. No zero-distance
assumption or optimization claim is needed.

For the earlier example $h=1+i$, $r=i$, $t=-1+i$, the inverse relation is
$-i$. Forward under $i$ and reverse under $-i$ both score 2; the unwanted
directions score −2. This achieves the directional inverse distinction that
DistMult cannot make. Untied learned relation rows do not automatically become
conjugates; that remains a property to encourage or inspect.

### Multiple tails and composition still depend on the score condition

Fix a transformed head $hr=-1+i$. The two distinct tails $-1+i$ and $-2$
both give real alignment 2: their real coordinate pairs lie on the line
$-u+v=2$. Thus ComplEx can give several distinct tails the same high score,
just as the real dot-product model can. It does not ask all good tails to
equal the transformed head.

That same distinction blocks an automatic path-substitution argument. The
DistMult composition counterexample also works inside ComplEx by choosing all
imaginary components zero. Consequently, multiplying relation coordinates is
not by itself a guarantee that high path scores imply a high endpoint score.
This is a counterexample to a universal implication, not a claim that ComplEx
cannot fit data containing composition patterns. Expressiveness comparisons
must retain these explicit assumptions.

## 7. Optional extension: RotatE connects the two geometric ideas {#extension-rotate-turns-each-coordinate}

TransE predicts a point and measures the miss. ComplEx uses complex multiplication
and measures compatibility. **RotatE** combines parts of these ideas: it rotates
the head and measures the distance to the tail. It extends our four core models
and is the second model implemented in Lab 4.

Constrain each relation coordinate to magnitude one. It can turn a point without
stretching its distance from the origin. An angle specifies that turn. The
experiment below sets the tail to the forward landing point, then asks whether
the same relation can bring us back.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-rotate.html >}}

At 90 degrees, applying the relation twice makes a half-turn. The return landing
point differs from the head, so forward and reverse scores differ. At 180 degrees,
applying the same relation twice makes a full turn. Both directions fit, even
though the two entity points are distinct. This solves the symmetric-pair
construction that caused TransE's exact-fit collapse.

Now enable the inverse relation. It negates the return angle, so every chosen
forward turn can be undone. Symmetry and inversion are different: symmetry uses
the same relation in both directions; inversion allows a different relation.

$$
r_i=\cos\theta_i+i\sin\theta_i,\qquad
f(h,r,t)=-\|\mathbf h\circ\mathbf r-\mathbf t\|_2.
$$ {#eq-w04-rotate}

Here $\theta_i$ is coordinate $i$'s angle in radians, so $|r_i|=1$.
Each complex coordinate rotates independently. The norm combines all residual
coordinate magnitudes into one distance; the minus sign restores higher-is-better.
We use $\|\mathbf z\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_i|z_i|^2}$, matching our lab. Other
implementations can use a different norm, so reproduction requires checking it.

Using the earlier $h=1+i$, $r=i$, $t=-1+i$ example, RotatE gives forward score
0 and reverse score $-2\sqrt2$. ComplEx gave 2 and −2 for the same coordinates.
The ranking agrees here, but the models measure different quantities. The choice
of complex numbers alone does not define a scorer.

::: {#prp-rotate .proposition name="Rotations compose by adding angles"}
If $\mathbf b=\mathbf a\circ\mathbf r_1$ and
$\mathbf c=\mathbf b\circ\mathbf r_2$, then
$\mathbf c=\mathbf a\circ(\mathbf r_1\circ\mathbf r_2)$.
The combined rotation multiplies relation coordinates, or equivalently adds
their angles modulo $2\pi$.
:::

Translations also compose: their vectors add. Neither identity proves that a
trained model obeys every logical rule over its high-scoring triples. And one
exact RotatE landing point still cannot equal two distinct tail vectors. Nearby
tails can score well; an exact multiple-tail fit would make them coincide.

::: {.predict}
**Compare, then explain.** A graph contains symmetric roommate relations and
directed advisor relations. Which fixed limitation rules out DistMult if both
directions must be distinguished? Why does a half-turn help RotatE?

::: {.predict-answer}
DistMult forces equal scores on every reversed pair. RotatE can use a half-turn
for the symmetric relation and a different angle for a directed relation. This
shows representational possibilities; validation must still test whether learning
finds useful parameters.
:::
:::

## 8. Learning turns geometric choices into a model

### Compare an observed fact with a sampled alternative

All our coordinates so far were chosen by hand. Training starts with adjustable
entity and relation parameters, then repeatedly asks an observed fact to outscore
a sampled alternative. Over many comparisons, the shared parameters organize
the graph in the chosen geometry.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-training.html >}}

To make a comparison, keep the relation and replace either the head or the tail.
Replacing Innopolis with Kazan changes the claim while preserving the question
being asked. Such a **corruption** gives the model something to discriminate.
Because the graph is incomplete, a sampled alternative can be an unrecorded truth
or even another known true answer. A training filter can reject known training
positives; it cannot discover every missing truth.

### Correct ordering needs enough separation

Suppose the observed triple has distance 1 and the sampled alternative has
distance 1.5. The observed triple already wins. A **margin** of 1 asks it to win
by a full unit, so the separation is still short by 0.5.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-margin.html >}}

Move the negative distance until the loss first reaches zero, then increase the
margin. Notice that the boundary moves. This loss rewards a specified gap, not
an absolute demand that every positive distance become zero.

$$
\ell=\max(0,\gamma-f_{\mathrm{pos}}+f_{\mathrm{neg}}),
\qquad \mathcal L=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\ell_b.
$$ {#eq-w04-margin}

The positive and negative scores belong to one comparison, $\gamma>0$ is the
required margin, and $B$ is the number of comparisons averaged in a batch.
With negative-distance scores, the loss is
$\max(0,\gamma+d_{\mathrm{pos}}-d_{\mathrm{neg}})$.
The example above gives $\max(0,1+1-1.5)=0.5$.

::: {.predict}
**Catch a reversed objective.** Someone proposes a loss that gets smaller when
the negative score increases. Would optimizing it improve the desired ranking?

::: {.predict-answer}
No. A larger negative score makes the sampled alternative more competitive.
Our loss should decrease when the positive score increases, or when the negative
score decreases. Checking that direction catches a sign error before training.
:::
:::

### Updating a shared vector changes several facts

Gradient descent adjusts parameters to reduce the loss. For an active comparison,
it tries to improve the positive score relative to the negative score. With tail
corruption, the head and relation occur in both scores, so their updates combine
both influences. One parameter change can also affect other facts that reuse
the same entity or relation. Training balances those coupled requirements.

### Follow one gradient update by hand {#one-gradient-update}

A one-dimensional example makes those two influences visible. Let head $h=0$,
relation $r=0$, observed tail $t=2$, and sampled tail $n=-1$. The predicted
location is $q=h+r=0$. Positive and negative distances are 2 and 1, so margin
1 gives loss $1+2-1=2$. The sampled alternative currently wins.

While the margin is active, the loss is
$1+|h+r-t|-|h+r-n|$. Its two residuals are −2 and 1. The derivative of
$|x|$ at a nonzero $x$ is its sign. Therefore the gradient with respect to the
shared prediction is $-1-(+1)=-2$: moving the prediction right both approaches
the observed tail and moves away from the sampled one. Since $q=h+r$, both
$h$ and $r$ receive that gradient.

Take one gradient-descent step with learning rate 0.1, updating all four
parameters together. This illustration uses no normalization during the step.

| Parameter | Before | Gradient | After subtracting 0.1 × gradient |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Head $h$ | 0 | −2 | 0.2 |
| Relation $r$ | 0 | −2 | 0.2 |
| Observed tail $t$ | 2 | 1 | 1.9 |
| Sampled tail $n$ | −1 | 1 | −1.1 |

The new prediction is $0.2+0.2=0.4$. Both distances are now 1.5: the positive
score improved from −2 to −1.5, and the negative score fell from −1 to −1.5.
The loss fell from 2 to $1+1.5-1.5=1$. We have improved the comparison without
yet satisfying the margin. This is what one local optimization step achieves;
other triples sharing these rows may respond differently.

If you differentiate only the positive score when updating the head or relation,
you miss half the signal in this example. If you forget the minus sign on the
negative distance, you move the prediction toward both tails. Following a small
update is therefore a stronger implementation check than merely observing a
loss value printed by a training loop.

::: {.w4-thesis}
**TransE training in outline.** Given training triples and adjustable embeddings:

1. Apply the chosen normalization rule; our lab normalizes entity rows at the start of each epoch.
2. Take a batch of observed triples and sample head or tail replacements.
3. Score the observations and their sampled alternatives using the same parameters.
4. Measure the average shortfall from the desired margin.
5. Differentiate that loss and update the shared parameters.
6. Repeat for the remaining batches.
:::

Normalization, negative sampling, initialization, and optimization settings are
part of the training recipe. They can change the outcome even when the scorer
is unchanged. Our normalization schedule is a teaching variant, not an exact
reproduction of every original paper. The closing algorithms specify a second
recipe with explicit regularization and checks for each step.

The training loss answers whether sampled comparisons are improving. It does
not yet tell us how well the model ranks missing facts. That requires a separate
test with parameters held fixed.

## 9. Evaluation asks whether the right answers rise to the top

### A question can have more than one true answer

Consider the held-out fact “the Volga flows through Tatarstan.” We ask
$(\text{Volga},\text{flows\_through},?)$ and score every entity as a tail.
In the toy model below, Russia ranks above Tatarstan. Russia is also a known
true answer. Should that count as a mistake on this target fact?

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-eval.html >}}

::: {#def-w04-filtered .definition name="Filtered evaluation"}
For a target triple, **filtered evaluation** excludes other known true answers
to the same query before measuring the target's rank. The target itself remains
eligible. The model's scores do not change.
:::

Filtering separates two questions: whether the target outranks incorrect
alternatives, and whether it outranks another correct answer. In this example,
removing Russia moves Tatarstan from rank 2 to rank 1. Filtering cannot remove
an unrecorded truth, and it does not remove a higher-scoring incorrect answer
just because that answer is inconvenient.

### Ties need an explicit rule

If candidate scores are $[9,8,8,1]$ and the target is one of the 8s, it occupies
positions 2 and 3 jointly with another candidate. We use their average position,
2.5. Giving every tied target the best position would make a model that ties
everything look far better than it should.

$$
\rho=1+n_{>}+\frac{n_{=}-1}{2}.
$$ {#eq-w04-rank}

Count only eligible candidates after filtering. Here $n_{>}$ counts scores
strictly above the target and $n_{=}$ counts scores equal to the target,
including the target itself. The subtraction removes that self-count. With
no ties, $n_{=}=1$ and the formula becomes ordinary one-based rank.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-rank.html >}}

First turn filtering on for the Volga example and explain the excluded row.
Then choose the tie example. If the score-9 candidate is another known true
answer, filtering leaves the two 8s in positions 1 and 2. The target's average
rank is now 1.5, not 1.

### Summarize ranks without changing their meaning

For target ranks 2 and 1, the reciprocal ranks are $1/2$ and $1$. Their mean is
0.75. One of the two targets is first, so Hits@1 is 0.5. Both are in the first
two positions, so Hits@2 is 1.

$$
\mathrm{MRR}=\frac1Q\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac1{\rho_q},\qquad
\mathrm{Hits@}K=\frac1Q\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\mathbf1[\rho_q\leq K].
$$ {#eq-w04-metrics}

$Q$ counts queries, $\rho_q$ is a target's rank, and $K$ is the cutoff.
The indicator contributes one when its condition holds and zero otherwise.
We apply the same formulas to fractional average ranks and report that convention.
Both head and tail prediction produce a query, so each held-out triple contributes
two ranks in our lab.

::: {.w4-thesis}
**Evaluation in outline.** With the trained parameters fixed:

1. Hide the tail and score every entity as a candidate.
2. Exclude other known true tails, preserving the target.
3. Count better and tied candidates to obtain the target's rank.
4. Hide the head and repeat the same procedure for head prediction.
5. Collect these ranks across held-out triples, then calculate MRR and Hits@K.
:::

Use validation data to choose the model and its settings; reserve the test data
for evaluation after those choices. A training rejection filter normally sees
training truths. A conventional final benchmark evaluation filter can include
train, validation, and test truths because it adjusts metric accounting without
updating parameters. Keep those purposes separate.

Candidate scope matters too. Ranking against a few easy alternatives or a
restricted entity type is a different task from ranking against every entity.
And if a test fact's inverse is already in training, a lookup can masquerade as
generalization. FB15k-237 reduces the common inverse leakage found in FB15k.
The split and evaluation protocol deserve as much attention as the model name.

## 10. Choose a model by the distinction the task needs

We can now return to the relation patterns and ask a more precise question than
“Which model is best?” What must the model distinguish for this graph, and what
does its scorer make easy or impossible?

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-patterns.html >}}

Begin with one relation, not the entire comparison at once. A directed relation
requires different scores for a reversed pair, which rules out DistMult for that
distinction. Two distinct tails with an exact projected fit suggest why TransR
may help. ComplEx can express symmetric scores with real relation coordinates
and allow asymmetric scores with imaginary relation coordinates. These arguments
guide experiments; they do not replace
validation on held-out facts.

### The four core models: space determines the available distinctions {#four-models-space-and-expressiveness}

Read each row as a design decision followed by its consequence. Here $d$ is
the entity dimension and $k$ is the TransR relation dimension. A construction
shows that a model **can** represent a pattern under stated conditions; an
identity such as DistMult's symmetry holds for **every** parameter setting.

::: {.w4-table-scroll}
| Model | Embedding space and operation | What this makes possible | What to check before choosing it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TransE** | Entities and relations in $\mathbb R^d$; add a relation vector | Direction; inverse shifts; additive composition of exact translations | Exact symmetric pairs or several exact tails force entity vectors to coincide |
| **TransR** | Entities in $\mathbb R^d$; $M_r\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}$; relation shift in $\mathbb R^k$ | Relation-specific views; distinct entities can share a projection; direction and inverses | The matrix must have a nontrivial kernel to hide differences; arbitrary projections do not automatically compose |
| **DistMult** | Entities and relations in $\mathbb R^d$; weighted coordinate products | Symmetric compatibility; several distinct tails can score highly | Reversing the endpoints always preserves the score; directed inverses cannot fix that identity |
| **ComplEx** | Entities and relations in $\mathbb C^d$; real part of a product with the conjugated tail | Symmetric or asymmetric compatibility; inverse scores by conjugating the relation; multiple high-scoring tails | High scores on a path do not by themselves guarantee a high score for its composed relation |
:::

For TransR, the [composition construction](#transr-composition-proof) deliberately
discards the directions lost along either step. For DistMult and ComplEx,
relation products can be useful in rule mining, but are not a universal logical
implication between high-scoring triples. For TransE, “collapse” concerns an
**exact zero-distance fit**; it does not say that approximate symmetric or
multiple-tail rankings are impossible. Keep these assumptions attached to the
comparison when explaining expressiveness.

Keep comparisons fair. The same complex dimension stores twice as many real
entity numbers as a real dimension. TransR adds a matrix per relation. Give
models comparable parameter and optimization budgets, use the same candidate
sets and filters, and inspect performance by relation when possible.

### Compare the parameter budget as well as the model name {#model-parameter-cost}

The table counts stored **real numbers**, so complex models are compared on
the same basis. Here $d$ is the number of entity coordinates in the model's
own space; for ComplEx and RotatE these are complex coordinates. TransR has
$k$ coordinates in relation space. The work column concerns one triple score,
before scoring all candidates or differentiating a batch.

::: {.w4-table-scroll}
| Model | Per entity | Per relation | Work per score |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| TransE | $d$ | $d$ | $O(d)$ |
| TransR | $d$ | $kd+k$ | $O(kd)$ |
| DistMult | $d$ | $d$ | $O(d)$ |
| ComplEx | $2d$ | $2d$ | $O(d)$ |
| RotatE | $2d$ | $d$ angles | $O(d)$ |
:::

Multiply the entity column by $n_e$ and the relation column by $n_r$ to obtain
the parameter count, excluding optimizer state. For 10,000 entities, 100 real
coordinates require one million real entity parameters; 100 complex coordinates
require two million. Reducing the complex dimension to 50 matches that entity
budget, although it does not make the models equivalent. TransR's matrix cost
can become substantial when there are many relation types.

Candidate ranking adds another factor: a simple all-entity query evaluates
$n_e$ candidate triples. Batching, cached projections for a fixed relation,
and matrix multiplication can improve the implementation, but do not change
what the scorer represents. An apparently better model can also have received
more parameters, more negative samples, or more optimization. Those differences
belong in an experimental comparison.

### Read the benchmark result as a question about the data {#stanford-benchmark-comparison}

The following figure compares historical MRR values on FB15k-237 and WN18RR.
Treat them as a worked
example of reading evidence, not a current leaderboard or a result produced
by our walkthrough.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-benchmark.html >}}

TransE exceeds DistMult on FB15k-237 in this table, but their order reverses
on WN18RR. RotatE has the largest MRR among the listed models on both. The
first observation warns against choosing a model by one dataset's ranking;
the second gives a result to investigate, not proof that the same winner must
appear under every graph, dimension, sampler, or training budget.

For completeness, these are the other reported metrics from the same source.
MR is mean rank, so smaller is better; MRR and Hits@10 are larger-is-better.
The source leaves TransR's results blank, so there is no TransR measurement
to infer from that row.

::: {.w4-table-scroll}
| Model | FB15k-237 MR | MRR | Hits@10 | WN18RR MR | MRR | Hits@10 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| TransE | 357 | .294 | .465 | 3384 | .226 | .501 |
| DistMult | 254 | .241 | .419 | 5110 | .430 | .490 |
| ComplEx | 339 | .247 | .428 | 5261 | .440 | .510 |
| RotatE | 177 | .338 | .533 | 3340 | .476 | .571 |
:::

These historical values come from PDF page 62 of the [source lecture](#lecture-attribution).
That table alone
does not specify every training and evaluation setting needed to reproduce them.

Why can mean rank and MRR disagree about a model? Compare query ranks
$[1,100]$ with $[10,10]$. The first model's mean rank is 50.5, worse than 10,
but its MRR is $(1+0.01)/2=0.505$, better than 0.1. Mean rank is sensitive to
large-rank failures; reciprocal rank emphasizes getting answers near the top.
This is why a single metric can hide a different distribution of successes
and failures.

To investigate a model difference, begin with training-data relation statistics:
which relations show reciprocal edges, which have many observed tails per head,
and which have known inverses? Missing reverse edges are not automatically
evidence of asymmetry, so interpret these as observations about the available
graph. Then evaluate by relation or pattern group on held-out facts under the
same protocol. The geometry suggests a hypothesis about where a model may
struggle; the grouped experiment checks that hypothesis.

::: {.predict}
**Explain a ranking reversal.** In the historical table, TransE has a better
WN18RR mean rank than DistMult but a worse MRR. What kind of query-level results
could produce that pattern? What extra result would you request before choosing?

::: {.predict-answer}
TransE could avoid some extremely bad ranks while DistMult places more answers
very near the top. Request the rank distribution or per-relation metrics,
together with matched training and evaluation settings. The aggregate numbers
do not identify a unique explanation.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Three mistakes to recognize"}
**A small distance means a low-quality fact.** Our distance scorers negate the
distance, so a smaller miss gives a higher score.

**A more powerful optimizer will fix a symmetric scorer.** DistMult's reversal
identity holds for every parameter setting. The required distinction must be
available in the model itself.

**A high completion score proves a rule.** A learned ranking can suggest a fact.
A proof also needs the relevant premises and an explicit valid inference rule.
:::

## 11. Algorithms you can implement and check {#algorithms-you-can-implement}

We have drawn the spaces, calculated scores, and explained their consequences.
Now turn those ideas into procedures. Keep the following division of labor in
mind: **the model defines the score; the training recipe learns its parameters;
the evaluation protocol measures its ranking.** Changing the optimizer cannot
remove an identity such as DistMult's symmetry.

The four scoring algorithms below are followed by a negative sampler, a complete
training loop, and filtered evaluation. Read a scorer together with its small
check before trying a full training run. Implement the steps first on a tiny
graph, then report both validation and test rankings. The worked calculations
below give you expected results before you need a larger dataset.

### One interface, four scoring algorithms

An input triple contains integer IDs $(h,r,t)$. $E[h]$ means “look up entity
row $h$,” and $R[r]$ means “look up relation row $r$.” **Do not multiply the
IDs themselves.** All four algorithms return one real score $s$, with higher
better. On a batch of $B$ triples, repeat the calculation independently across
the batch to return $B$ scores; sum coordinates, never batch examples.

::: {#alg-w04-score-transe .algorithm name="Score a triple with TransE"}
**Input:** $(h,r,t)$; entity table $E\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times d}$;
relation table $R\in\mathbb R^{n_r\times d}$. **Output:** real score $s$.

1. **Look up** $\mathbf h\leftarrow E[h]$, $\mathbf r\leftarrow R[r]$, $\mathbf t\leftarrow E[t]$.
2. **Translate** $\mathbf q\leftarrow\mathbf h+\mathbf r$.
3. **Measure the residual** $\boldsymbol\delta\leftarrow\mathbf q-\mathbf t$.
4. **Return** $s\leftarrow-\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^d\delta_j^2}$.
:::

**Trace it.** With $\mathbf h=(1,1)$ and $\mathbf r=(2,1)$, the prediction is
$(3,2)$. Candidate tails $(3,2)$, $(3,1)$, and $(0,6)$ have residual lengths
0, 1, and 5, so their scores are **0, −1, −5**. The first candidate wins.
Every score is at most zero; an exact fit scores zero. Forgetting the minus
sign would rank the farthest candidate first. One score costs $O(d)$ operations.

::: {#alg-w04-score-transr .algorithm name="Score a triple with TransR"}
**Input:** $(h,r,t)$; $E\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times d}$;
$R\in\mathbb R^{n_r\times k}$; $M\in\mathbb R^{n_r\times k\times d}$.
**Output:** real score $s$.

1. **Look up** $\mathbf h\leftarrow E[h]$, $\mathbf r\leftarrow R[r]$, $\mathbf t\leftarrow E[t]$, $A\leftarrow M[r]$.
2. **Project both endpoints** $\mathbf h_\perp\leftarrow A\mathbf h$ and $\mathbf t_\perp\leftarrow A\mathbf t$.
3. **Translate in relation space** $\boldsymbol\delta\leftarrow\mathbf h_\perp+\mathbf r-\mathbf t_\perp$.
4. **Return** $s\leftarrow-\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^k\delta_j^2}$.
:::

**Trace it.** Use $d=2$, $k=1$, $A=[1\;0]$, $\mathbf h=(0,0)$, and
$\mathbf r=(2)$. Tails $(2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$ both project to $(2)$ and score
**0**, while $(-1,0)$ scores **−3**. The two correct tails remain distinct
in the entity table. A rectangular matrix is a useful test: it catches an
accidental transpose that a square identity matrix could hide. Both endpoints
must use the **same matrix selected by this triple's relation**. Cost: $O(kd)$.

::: {#alg-w04-score-distmult .algorithm name="Score a triple with DistMult"}
**Input:** $(h,r,t)$; $E\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times d}$;
$R\in\mathbb R^{n_r\times d}$. **Output:** real score $s$.

1. **Look up** $\mathbf h\leftarrow E[h]$, $\mathbf r\leftarrow R[r]$, $\mathbf t\leftarrow E[t]$.
2. **Weight the head coordinates** $\mathbf q\leftarrow\mathbf h\circ\mathbf r$.
3. **Return** $s\leftarrow\sum_{j=1}^d q_jt_j$.
:::

**Trace it.** With $\mathbf h=(2,1)$, $\mathbf r=(1,3)$, and
$\mathbf t=(1,2)$, the weighted head is $(2,3)$ and the score is
$2\cdot1+3\cdot2=\mathbf8$. Reversing head and tail also gives **8**.
That equality is a required property of a correct implementation. A different
reverse score would be a bug, even if it appeared useful for a directed relation.
The score is not a distance and need not be negative. Cost: $O(d)$.

::: {#alg-w04-score-complex .algorithm name="Score a triple with ComplEx using real arithmetic"}
**Input:** $(h,r,t)$; real and imaginary tables $E_{\mathrm{re}},E_{\mathrm{im}}
\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times d}$ and $R_{\mathrm{re}},R_{\mathrm{im}}
\in\mathbb R^{n_r\times d}$. **Output:** real score $s$.

1. **Look up** $\mathbf h=\mathbf a+i\mathbf b$, $\mathbf r=\mathbf c+i\mathbf d$, $\mathbf t=\mathbf u+i\mathbf v$ from their paired rows.
2. **Multiply head and relation:** $\mathbf x\leftarrow\mathbf a\circ\mathbf c-\mathbf b\circ\mathbf d$ and $\mathbf y\leftarrow\mathbf a\circ\mathbf d+\mathbf b\circ\mathbf c$.
3. **Conjugate the tail conceptually:** $\overline{\mathbf t}=\mathbf u-i\mathbf v$.
4. **Return the real part:** $s\leftarrow\sum_{j=1}^d(x_ju_j+y_jv_j)$.
:::

**Why the last sign is positive.** Multiplication gives
$(x+iy)(u-iv)=(xu+yv)+i(yu-xv)$. The two imaginary factors produce
$i(-i)=+1$. This is exactly where forgetting the conjugate changes the scorer.
